interest: This file provides rare insight into the postwar mechanics of global document exploitation, detailing how Nisei units, intelligence agencies, and scholars surveyed, salvaged, and microfilmed Japanese diplomatic archives across multiple continents. It captures early Cold War diplomatic maneuvering, revealing how the United States resisted Soviet demands for quadripartite control over Tokyo records while asserting unilateral authority over captured enemy materials. Furthermore, the documents illuminate significant intelligence revelations—such as the Japanese decipherment of State Department traffic via a stolen consular cipher key in Taihoku—and record the administrative origins of the pre-war Japanese Foreign Office microfilm collection that remains vital to modern diplomatic history.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)
overview: This file documents the postwar custody, inventorying, microfilming, and disposition of Japanese diplomatic and consular archives, government property, and personal effects by the United States and Allied powers between July 1946 and October 1949. Spanning diplomatic posts across Europe, Latin America, North America, and Asia, the records cover the impounding and liquidation of embassy property in capitals such as Rome, Lisbon, Buenos Aires, and Ottawa, alongside quadripartite negotiations and Cold War friction with the Soviet Union over central archives access. Most notably, the collection traces the inter-agency conception, funding, and execution of the joint State Department, SCAP, and Library of Congress project to survey and microfilm the Japanese Foreign Office archives in Tokyo under Glenn W. Shaw and Thomas C. Smith, establishing foundational policies that opened pre-World War II Japanese records to unrestricted historical research.
